claim: Oncogenic human papillomaviruses (HPV) are small DNA viruses that infect keratinocytes.
source: Oncogenic human papillomaviruses (HPV) are small DNA viruses that infect keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information about HPV.

claim: The tetraspanin CD151 and the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are important molecular players involved in virus entry.
source: Aside from the virus itself, important molecular players involved in virus entry include the tetraspanin CD151 and the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information.

claim: The proteinase ADAM17 activates the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) pathway by the shedding of growth factors.
source: We find that the proteinase ADAM17 activates the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) pathway by the shedding of growth factors which triggers the formation of an endocytic entry platform.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ADAM17-mediated growth factor shedding triggers the formation of an endocytic entry platform.
source: We find that the proteinase ADAM17 activates the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) pathway by the shedding of growth factors which triggers the formation of an endocytic entry platform.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Infectious endocytic entry platforms carrying virus particles consist of two-fold larger CD151 domains containing the EGFR.
source: Infectious endocytic entry platforms carrying virus particles consist of two-fold larger CD151 domains containing the EGFR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by STED microscopy data in Figure 4.

claim: Initial virus binding is dissected from ADAM17-dependent assembly of a HPV/CD151/EGFR entry platform.
source: Our finding clearly dissects initial virus binding from ADAM17-dependent assembly of a HPV/CD151/EGFR entry platform.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing ADAM17 independence of virus binding but dependence for platform assembly.

claim: More than 240 papillomavirus types have been characterized in diverse hosts, including mammals, birds and reptiles.
source: More than 240 papillomavirus types have been characterized in diverse hosts, including mammals, birds and reptiles.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Oncogenic HPV types 16, 18, and 31 are responsible for severe human cancers, including cervical cancer and anogenital, head and neck tumors.
source: For instance, the oncogenic HPV types 16, 18, and 31 are responsible for severe human cancers, including cervical cancer and anogenital, head and neck tumors (Doorbar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HPV infections require a micro-wound enabling virion binding to mitotically active basal keratinocytes.
source: HPV infections require a micro-wound enabling virion binding to mitotically active basal keratinocytes (Doorbar et al., 2012; Ozbun, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Virus internalization is asynchronous and slow, with a halftime of several hours.
source: However, virus internalization is asynchronous and slow, with a halftime of several hours (Sapp and Bienkowska-Haba, 2009; Becker et al., 2018; Schelhaas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TAPI-0 and GW280264X diminished HPV16 infection in HaCaT keratinocytes.
source: TAPI-0 and GW diminished infection, whereas the ADAM10 inhibitor GI showed no significant effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ADAM10 inhibitor GI254023X showed no significant effect on HPV16 infection.
source: TAPI-0 and GW diminished infection, whereas the ADAM10 inhibitor GI showed no significant effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ADAM17 depletion consistently and strongly decreased HPV16 infection in HeLa cells, HaCaT cells, and primary normal human epithelial keratinocytes (NHEK).
source: Under all conditions ADAM17 depletion consistently and strongly decreased infection (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C with siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: ADAM10 depletion showed no clear effect on HPV16 infection.
source: In contrast, ADAM10 depletion showed no clear effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: ADAM17 is required for infection by HPV18 and HPV31.
source: ADAM17 was also required for the infection by two other highly oncogenic HPV types, HPV18 and HPV31 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ADAM17 is important for the infection with oncogenic human papillomaviruses.
source: Altogether, this indicates that ADAM17 is important for the infection with oncogenic human papillomaviruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing ADAM17 requirement for HPV16, 18, and 31 infection.

claim: Directly after virus incubation, virus particles associated with the cell surface poorly overlapped with CD151-enriched domains.
source: Directly after virus incubation (marked as time point 0:00), we found virus particles associated with the cell surface, but they poorly overlapped with CD151-enriched domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: One hour after adding PsVs, there was a moderate increase in CD151-L1 overlap that further increased in the next 2 hr.
source: One hour after adding PsVs (corresponds to time point 0:45), there was a moderate increase in CD151-L1 overlap that further increased in the next 2 hr, apparently plateauing after about 5 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time course microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average size of a CD151 cluster is roughly 200 nm.
source: The average size of a CD151 cluster is roughly 200 nm (see Figure 4), and an HPV particle has a size of 55 nm (Baker et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4 and cited literature for HPV particle size.

claim: An HPV particle has a size of 55 nm.
source: The average size of a CD151 cluster is roughly 200 nm (see Figure 4), and an HPV particle has a size of 55 nm (Baker et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Baker et al., 1991.

claim: The fraction of PsVs in close proximity to CD151 nanoclusters strongly increases over time.
source: Interestingly, we uncovered a large fraction of PsVs in close proximity to CD151 nano-clusters already directly after virus binding. The fraction of such closely associated viral particles strongly increases over time (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The CD151 brightness at the site of viral particle binding increases over time.
source: Importantly, as well the CD151 brightness at the site of viral particle binding increases (Figure 2C), suggesting that the viral particle enriches CD151 in preparation of endocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Viral particles are almost immobile when attached to the cell body.
source: Because viral particles are almost immobile when attached to the cell body, as intensively investigated and discussed before (Schelhaas et al., 2008), we suggest that CD151 is recruited to the virus binding site.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work by Schelhaas et al., 2008.

claim: CD151 is recruited to the virus binding site.
source: Because viral particles are almost immobile when attached to the cell body, as intensively investigated and discussed before (Schelhaas et al., 2008), we suggest that CD151 is recruited to the virus binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that viral particles are immobile while CD151 intensity increases at virus binding sites.

claim: Only in the presence of ADAM17, PsVs trigger the internalization of preferentially larger CD151 clusters.
source: Only in the presence of ADAM17, PsVs trigger the internalization of preferentially larger clusters.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data on membrane sheets shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proximity ligation assay shows an ADAM17-dependent close association between viral particles and CD151.
source: Besides, the proximity ligation assay shows an ADAM17-dependent close association between viral particles and CD151.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: ADAM17 neither affects virus binding to the cell surface, nor influences the release of L1 protein.
source: In contrast, ADAM17 neither affects virus binding to the cell surface, nor influences the release of L1 protein.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and western blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: ADAM17 acts after virus primary binding/release.
source: First, ADAM17 acts after virus primary binding/release, because infection is almost blocked in ADAM17-depleted recipient cells, receiving viral particles from control donor cells.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ADAM17-depleted donor cells infect at a lesser extent their respective recipient cells.
source: The second observation is that ADAM17-depleted donor cells infect at a lesser extent their respective recipient cells, and in parallel, that control donor cells are less infected when recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: Control donor cells are less infected when recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted.
source: The second observation is that ADAM17-depleted donor cells infect at a lesser extent their respective recipient cells, and in parallel, that control donor cells are less infected when recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: EGF increases the infection rate of ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Consistently, additional findings pointed toward an involvement of the EGFR as the receptor that mediates the action of these biomolecules. For example, EGF increases the infection rate of ADAM17-depleted cells, EGF increases the proximity between L1 and CD151 after ADAM17 knockdown, and ADAM17 knockdown diminishes the overlap between L1 and EGFR.
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EGF increases the proximity between L1 and CD151 after ADAM17 knockdown.
source: For example, EGF increases the infection rate of ADAM17-depleted cells, EGF increases the proximity between L1 and CD151 after ADAM17 knockdown, and ADAM17 knockdown diminishes the overlap between L1 and EGFR.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: ADAM17 knockdown diminishes the overlap between L1 and EGFR.
source: For example, EGF increases the infection rate of ADAM17-depleted cells, EGF increases the proximity between L1 and CD151 after ADAM17 knockdown, and ADAM17 knockdown diminishes the overlap between L1 and EGFR.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: ADAM17 depletion reduces the amount of AREG in the supernatant of HaCaT cells.
source: We find less AREG and TGF-α in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells, corroborated by a reduction of the infection rate after treatment with AREG and TGF-α neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ADAM17 depletion reduces the amount of TGF-α in the supernatant of cells.
source: We find less AREG and TGF-α in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells, corroborated by a reduction of the infection rate after treatment with AREG and TGF-α neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by ectodomain shedding assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Treatment with AREG neutralizing antibodies reduces HPV16 infection rate.
source: We find less AREG and TGF-α in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells, corroborated by a reduction of the infection rate after treatment with AREG and TGF-α neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Treatment with TGF-α neutralizing antibodies reduces HPV16 infection rate.
source: We find less AREG and TGF-α in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells, corroborated by a reduction of the infection rate after treatment with AREG and TGF-α neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Adding AREG, TGF-α, and HB-EGF to the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells increases ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
source: Adding ADAM17 cleavage products such as AREG, TGF-α, and HB-EGF to the supernatant of serum-starved or ADAM17-depleted cells increases ERK1/2 phosphorylation and infection.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Adding AREG, TGF-α, and HB-EGF to the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells increases infection.
source: Adding ADAM17 cleavage products such as AREG, TGF-α, and HB-EGF to the supernatant of serum-starved or ADAM17-depleted cells increases ERK1/2 phosphorylation and infection.
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: ADAM17 sheds soluble biomolecules like HB-EGF, TGF-α, and AREG, which leads to activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway and successful HPV16 infection.
source: These findings show that ADAM17 sheds soluble biomolecules like HB-EGF, TGF-α, and AREG, which leads to activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway and successful HPV16 infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including ELISA, shedding assays, ERK phosphorylation, and infection assays.

claim: Cells with functional ADAM17 are susceptible for infection mediated by the cleavage of membrane-bound growth factor precursors.
source: In conclusion, cells with functional ADAM17, or cells in the neighborhood of such cells, are susceptible for infection mediated by the cleavage of membrane-bound growth factor precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-culture experiments and growth factor studies.

claim: Cells in the neighborhood of cells with functional ADAM17 are susceptible for infection.
source: In conclusion, cells with functional ADAM17, or cells in the neighborhood of such cells, are susceptible for infection mediated by the cleavage of membrane-bound growth factor precursors.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-culture transwell assay showing that bioactive molecules can act on neighboring cells.

claim: The GFs activate the ERK signaling pathway, a precondition for the maturation of viral particle-carrying CD151/EGFR clusters that function as entry platforms.
source: The GFs then activate the ERK signaling pathway, a precondition for the maturation of viral particle-carrying CD151/EGFR clusters that function as entry platforms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing ERK activation by GFs and the requirement of ERK signaling for platform formation.

claim: CD151 defines the entry receptor complex.
source: The tetraspanin CD151 defines the entry receptor complex (Scheffer et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: ADAM17 depletion reduced virus-CD151 overlap by roughly a third in HaCaTs or NHEK.
source: 5 hr after initial PsVs contact, we found a significant effect. ADAM17 depletion reduced virus-CD151 overlap by roughly a third in HaCaTs or NHEK (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: ADAM17 is not required for initial virus binding to the cell surface.
source: To investigate a role of ADAM17 in virus binding, we employed flow cytometry analysis testing whether ADAM17 depletion diminishes the number of PsVs on the cell surface, which was not the case (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). Therefore, we exclude ADAM17 requirement for initial virus binding to the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: L1 is not a substrate for ADAM17.
source: Investigating the activity of ADAM17 (using TGF-α as positive control) and the cleavage pattern of the viral L1 protein (L1 priming), we find that L1 is neither a substrate for ADAM17 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B) nor is internalization of viral particles efficiently inhibited by ADAM17 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Internalization of viral particles is not efficiently inhibited by ADAM17 depletion.
source: Investigating the activity of ADAM17 (using TGF-α as positive control) and the cleavage pattern of the viral L1 protein (L1 priming), we find that L1 is neither a substrate for ADAM17 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B) nor is internalization of viral particles efficiently inhibited by ADAM17 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by proteinase K protection assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C-D.

claim: L1 cleavage products substantially decreased in ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Instead, L1 cleavage products substantially decreased in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E and F.

claim: ADAM17 activity is required for viral particle association with L1-priming proteases such as kallikrein-8 prior to endocytosis.
source: Therefore, we speculate that ADAM17 activity is required for viral particle association with L1-priming proteases such as kallikrein-8 prior to endocytosis and additional proteases in intracellular compartments of the infectious entry pathway (Cerqueira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that L1 cleavage is reduced in ADAM17-depleted cells, with citation to Cerqueira et al., 2015.

claim: In HaCaT cells there is microscopic overlap between EGFR and L1.
source: As anticipated, in HaCaT cells we find microscopic overlap between EGFR and L1 (Figure 3A), which was significantly diminished in the absence of ADAM17 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EGFR-L1 overlap is significantly diminished in the absence of ADAM17.
source: As anticipated, in HaCaT cells we find microscopic overlap between EGFR and L1 (Figure 3A), which was significantly diminished in the absence of ADAM17 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: CD151 and EGFR co-enrich in membrane domains.
source: The similarity of the CD151 and EGFR localization patterns indicate co-enrichment of the two membrane proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: EGFR and CD151 overlap is independent of ADAM17.
source: Moreover, superresolution STED microscopy and quantitative analysis thereof revealed some overlap of the tetraspanin with EGFR (Figure 3D and E) in line with previous reports demonstrating that growth factor receptors are recruited into tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (Berditchevski and Odintsova, 2016; Zona et al., 2013; Bruening et al., 2018). However, overlap was independent of ADAM17 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ADAM17 is required for the association of HPV16 with the secondary entry receptor complex, which is composed of pre-formed CD151-EGFR nanocluster assemblies.
source: In conclusion, this indicates that ADAM17 is required for the association of HPV16 with the secondary entry receptor complex, which is composed of pre-formed CD151-EGFR nanocluster assemblies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing ADAM17-dependent virus-CD151 and virus-EGFR association, but ADAM17-independent CD151-EGFR association.

claim: CD151-enriched domains in PsVs-non-exposed cells have an average size of approximately 210 nm.
source: We find that CD151-enriched domains in PsVs-non-exposed cells have an average size of ≈ 210 nm (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy measurements on membrane sheets shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PsVs reduced the CD151 cluster diameter to approximately 150 nm.
source: PsVs reduced the cluster diameter to ≈ 150 nm, which is accompanied by a ≈ 25% reduction of the overall CD151 staining intensity (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy measurements on membrane sheets shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PsVs treatment is accompanied by approximately 25% reduction of the overall CD151 staining intensity.
source: PsVs reduced the cluster diameter to ≈ 150 nm, which is accompanied by a ≈ 25% reduction of the overall CD151 staining intensity (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy measurements on membrane sheets shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Reduction of cluster diameter and CD151 level both require ADAM17.
source: Reduction of cluster diameter and CD151 level both require ADAM17 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy measurements on membrane sheets shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Only in the presence of ADAM17, PsVs-CD151 entities are efficiently endocytosed.
source: Hence, the data indicate that only in the presence of ADAM17 PsVs-CD151 entities are efficiently endocytosed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD151 cluster size reduction and CD151 level reduction (indicators of endocytosis) require ADAM17.

claim: ADAM17 depletion in donor cells strongly diminished their infection.
source: As expected, ADAM17 depletion in donor cells strongly diminished their infection, but also halved the infection of non-ADAM17-depleted recipient cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ADAM17 depletion in donor cells halved the infection of non-ADAM17-depleted recipient cells.
source: As expected, ADAM17 depletion in donor cells strongly diminished their infection, but also halved the infection of non-ADAM17-depleted recipient cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Viral particles were released from donor cells and diffused to the recipient cells.
source: This demonstrates that virus particles were released from donor cells and diffused to the recipient cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-culture transwell assay where recipient cells become infected.

claim: The release of virus particles from primary attachment receptors does not require ADAM17.
source: We found no difference between control and ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 5D). This suggests that the release of virus particles from primary attachment receptors does not require ADAM17, which is in line with our previous finding where the quantity of surface bound virus particles was shown to be ADAM17-independent (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing no difference in L1 in supernatant shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Infection in recipient cells was almost completely blocked when ADAM17 was depleted in recipient cells receiving virus from non-depleted donor cells.
source: However, we observed the opposite, infection in recipient cells was almost completely blocked (Figure 5E, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Bioactive molecules are required for viral infection, no matter whether the viral particle is released and re-binds to the cell or not.
source: Hence, bioactive molecules are required for viral infection, no matter whether the viral particle is released and re-binds to the cell or not.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-culture experiments showing that ADAM17 in recipient cells is required for infection even when virus comes from control donors.

claim: Non-ADAM17-depleted donor cells are significantly less infected when the corresponding recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted.
source: The hypothesis on the involvement of released growth factors is supported by the observation that the non-ADAM17-depleted donor cells in the inverted assay configuration are significantly less infected when the corresponding recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted (Figure 5E, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Biomolecules act locally and do not diffuse over large distances.
source: However, the effect is small, suggesting that biomolecules rather act locally and do not diffuse over large distances.
evidence: This is inferred from the small effect on donor cells when recipient cells are ADAM17-depleted.

claim: Viral particles relatively fast rebind to cell surface receptors after release.
source: We further speculate that, although viral particles are released, they relatively fast rebind to cell surface receptors, explaining the large fraction of virus particles binding close to CD151 clusters already after 15 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that many viral particles are close to CD151 clusters shortly after binding.

claim: HPV16 infection requires activation of ERK signaling via EGFR.
source: The literature suggests a link between ADAM17 and infection pathways regulated via the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) ERK1/2 signaling pathway because HPV16 infection requires activation of ERK signaling via EGFR (Surviladze et al., 2012) and ADAM17 mediates cleavage of growth factors that activate ERK1/2 (Kansra et al., 2004; Göoz et al., 2006; Sommer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Surviladze et al., 2012.

claim: ADAM17 mediates cleavage of growth factors that activate ERK1/2.
source: The literature suggests a link between ADAM17 and infection pathways regulated via the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) ERK1/2 signaling pathway because HPV16 infection requires activation of ERK signaling via EGFR (Surviladze et al., 2012) and ADAM17 mediates cleavage of growth factors that activate ERK1/2 (Kansra et al., 2004; Göoz et al., 2006; Sommer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kansra et al., 2004; Göoz et al., 2006; Sommer et al., 2016.

claim: Cetuximab decreases HPV16 PsVs infection rate.
source: Thus, we used the EGFR blocking-antibody Cetuximab to confirm the functional requirement of EGFR in HPV16 PsVs infection (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In HaCaT cells ADAM17 depletion reduces ERK1/2 phosphorylation, independent from the treatment with PsVs.
source: We found that in HaCaT cells ADAM17 depletion reduces ERK1/2 phosphorylation, independent from the treatment with PsVs.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Supplying the medium with EGF abolished diminished ERK phosphorylation after ADAM17 depletion.
source: Supplying the medium with EGF did not only abolish diminished ERK phosphorylation after ADAM17 depletion (Figure 6A and B), but as well restored infection in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: EGF restored infection in ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Supplying the medium with EGF did not only abolish diminished ERK phosphorylation after ADAM17 depletion (Figure 6A and B), but as well restored infection in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EGF recovered the diminished CD151/L1 PLA signal in ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, EGF recovered the diminished CD151/L1 PLA signal in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Soluble biomolecules activate the ERK1/2 signaling pathway, a prerequisite for HPV16 entry platform formation and infection.
source: These findings show that soluble biomolecules activate the ERK1/2 signaling pathway, a prerequisite for HPV16 entry platform formation and infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing EGF rescue of ERK phosphorylation, infection, and platform formation.

claim: AREG was significantly reduced in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Both, AREG and TGF-α, were significantly reduced in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 7A and B), while HB-EGF was undetectable (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TGF-α was significantly reduced in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Both, AREG and TGF-α, were significantly reduced in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 7A and B), while HB-EGF was undetectable (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ectodomain shedding assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HB-EGF was undetectable in the supernatant.
source: Both, AREG and TGF-α, were significantly reduced in the supernatant of ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 7A and B), while HB-EGF was undetectable (not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Infection rates were significantly reduced when AREG neutralizing antibodies were added to the cells 1 hr before HPV16 PsVs addition.
source: Moreover, infection analyses showed that infection rates were significantly reduced when AREG or TGF-α neutralizing antibodies were added to the cells 1 hr before HPV16 PsVs addition (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Infection rates were significantly reduced when TGF-α neutralizing antibodies were added to the cells 1 hr before HPV16 PsVs addition.
source: Moreover, infection analyses showed that infection rates were significantly reduced when AREG or TGF-α neutralizing antibodies were added to the cells 1 hr before HPV16 PsVs addition (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Supplying the medium with HB-EGF, AREG, and TGF-α restored ERK phosphorylation in ADAM17-depleted cells.
source: Finally, we mimicked ADAM17 activity in ADAM17-depleted cells by adding the ADAM17 cleavage products HB-EGF, AREG, and TGF-α (Figure 7D–G). Supplying the medium with these GFs restored ERK phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: GF treatment increased infection rates in the absence as well as in the presence of ADAM17 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, GF treatment increased infection rates in the absence as well as in the presence of ADAM17 in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: The beneficial effect on infection rates was observed when the cells were grown under starvation conditions in the presence and in the absence of ADAM17.
source: The beneficial effect on infection rates was observed when the cells were grown under starvation conditions (in medium without FCS) in the presence (Figure 7F) and in the absence of ADAM17 (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Infection was not further supported by the addition of GFs if the cells were treated with control siRNA in full medium.
source: Infection was not further supported by the addition of GFs if the cells were treated with control siRNA in full medium (containing FCS) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) but was supported in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of GFs supported infection in ADAM17-depleted cells grown in full medium.
source: Infection was not further supported by the addition of GFs if the cells were treated with control siRNA in full medium (containing FCS) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) but was supported in ADAM17-depleted cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ADAM17 acts by releasing a subset of different GFs rather than a specific growth factor.
source: There is no specific growth factor. Instead ADAM17 acts by releasing a subset of different GFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that multiple GFs (AREG, TGF-α, HB-EGF) can rescue infection in ADAM17-depleted cells.

claim: Activation of ERK signaling is a precondition for the maturation of viral particle-carrying CD151/EGFR clusters that function as entry platforms.
source: The GFs then activate the ERK signaling pathway, a precondition for the maturation of viral particle-carrying CD151/EGFR clusters that function as entry platforms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing ERK activation by GFs and the requirement of ERK signaling for platform formation and infection.

claim: ADAM17-mediated release of GFs such as AREG, TGF-α or HB-EGF is an important step in infection with oncogenic papillomaviruses.
source: Our data suggest ADAM17-mediated release of GFs such as AREG, TGF-α or HB-EGF, known activators of ERK signaling as an important step in infection with oncogenic papillomaviruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing ADAM17-dependent GF release and their role in ERK activation and infection.

claim: CD151 is essential for viral endocytosis.
source: CD151 is essential for viral endocytosis (Spoden et al., 2008; Scheffer et al., 2013; Spoden et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2014; Fast et al., 2018) and co-internalizes with the virus via a clathrin-, caveolin-, and dynamin-independent endocytic pathway (Spoden et al., 2008; Spoden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: CD151 co-internalizes with the virus via a clathrin-, caveolin-, and dynamin-independent endocytic pathway.
source: CD151 is essential for viral endocytosis (Spoden et al., 2008; Scheffer et al., 2013; Spoden et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2014; Fast et al., 2018) and co-internalizes with the virus via a clathrin-, caveolin-, and dynamin-independent endocytic pathway (Spoden et al., 2008; Spoden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Growth factor receptors, in particular the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), were proposed as entry receptors for HPV16.
source: In addition, growth factor receptors (GFR), in particular the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), were proposed as entry receptors for HPV16 (Surviladze et al., 2012) and multiple other viruses such as vaccinia, cytomegalo, herpes simplex, influenza, and hepatitis C virus (Schäfer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Signal transduction like the activation of EGFR and ERK signaling is a prerequisite for HPV infection.
source: Moreover, signal transduction like the activation of EGFR and ERK signaling is a prerequisite for HPV infection (Schelhaas et al., 2012; Surviladze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Metalloproteases are involved early in HPV16 infection.
source: Recent data indicate that metalloproteases are involved early in HPV16 infection (Surviladze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Members of ADAM family regulate multiple cell signaling pathways by the release of bioactive proteins like GFR ligands.
source: From the many known metalloproteases, members of "A Disintegrin And Metalloprotease" (ADAMs) family regulate multiple cell signaling pathways by the release of bioactive proteins like GFR ligands (Gooz, 2010; Sahin et al., 2004; Horiuchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: ADAM10 and ADAM17 are highly expressed in keratinocytes.
source: From the ADAM family, ADAM10 and ADAM17 are the most likely candidates as they are highly expressed in keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2011; Maretzky et al., 2008; Sommer et al., 2016; Brooke et al., 2014; Hirayama et al., 2017) and involved in the shedding of numerous substrates (Reiss and Saftig, 2009; Edwards et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: ADAM10 and ADAM17 are involved in the shedding of numerous substrates.
source: From the ADAM family, ADAM10 and ADAM17 are the most likely candidates as they are highly expressed in keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2011; Maretzky et al., 2008; Sommer et al., 2016; Brooke et al., 2014; Hirayama et al., 2017) and involved in the shedding of numerous substrates (Reiss and Saftig, 2009; Edwards et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: CD151 moved fast while viral particles were clearly immobile in TIRF microscopy.
source: With TIRF microscopy, we studied the dynamics of viral particles and CD151. While viral particles were clearly immobile, CD151 moved fast (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD81 tetraspanin clusters are stable only for a few seconds.
source: These observations are in line with previous reports showing HPV16 PsV confinement on the cell body (Schelhaas et al., 2008) and that CD81 tetraspanin clusters are stable only for a few seconds (Homsi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Platform maturation presumably involves CD151 nucleation at viral particle binding sites.
source: However, if viral particles are stationary and tetraspanins are mobile (Espenel et al., 2008), platform maturation presumably involves CD151 nucleation at viral particle binding sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that viral particles are immobile and CD151 is mobile, with citation to Espenel et al., 2008.

claim: The increase in CD151 intensity at PsVs binding sites illustrates that CD151 nucleation is a slow process that can take up to several hours.
source: The increase in CD151 intensity at PsVs binding sites (Figure 2C) illustrates this is a slow process that can take up to several hours.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A reduction of the CD151 plasma membrane level after viral uptake is expected, as CD151 is co-internalized with viral particles.
source: A reduction of the CD151 plasma membrane level after viral uptake is expected, as CD151 is co-internalized with viral particles (Scheffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: A reduction from 210 to 150 nm corresponds to a halving of the area.
source: However, a reduction of the cluster diameter by a quarter corresponds to a halving of the area.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on the relationship between diameter and area.

claim: Reduction of the diameter in conjunction with a diminished CD151 level suggests the preferential internalization of larger CD151 clusters.
source: Moreover, reduction of the diameter in conjunction with a diminished CD151 level suggests the preferential internalization of larger CD151 clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both cluster size and CD151 level decrease after PsVs treatment.

claim: EGFR acts as a cofactor for HCV entry by promoting specific tetraspanin interactions with other proteins that result in the assembly of the HCV entry receptor complex.
source: In agreement with this, it has been recently shown that EGFR acts as a cofactor for HCV entry by promoting specific tetraspanin interactions with other proteins that result in the assembly of the HCV entry receptor complex (Zona et al., 2013; Bruening et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Tetraspanins are essential components of entry receptor complexes for corona-, influenza-, hepatitis C and other viruses.
source: This points toward a general scheme in viral uptake independent from the virus structure, further supported by the notion that tetraspanins stand for essential components of entry receptor complexes for corona-, influenza-, hepatitis C and other viruses (Zona et al., 2013; Earnest et al., 2015; Fast et al., 2017; Florin and Lang, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: GF/GFR complex formation and GFR-mediated ERK signaling is a prerequisite for the formation of virus-associated tetraspanin entry platforms for many types of viruses.
source: We propose a model in which GF/GFR complex formation and GFR-mediated ERK signaling is a prerequisite for the formation of virus-associated tetraspanin entry platforms for many types of viruses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings in this study and previous literature.

claim: GFR-dimerization triggered by the interaction of growth factors with its cognate receptors induces local accumulation of the associated tetraspanins, including CD151.
source: It seems plausible that the GFR-dimerization triggered by the interaction of growth factors with its cognate receptors induces local accumulation of the associated tetraspanins, including CD151.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed co-enrichment of EGFR and CD151.

claim: Clustering of cell factors might explain a more than two-fold increase in the CD151 microdomain size.
source: Thus, clustering of cell factors might explain a more than two-fold increase in the CD151 microdomain size and internalization of the virus-associated entry platform.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed increase in CD151 cluster size.

claim: Tetraspanin CD151 regulates integrin activities by influencing their positioning within tetraspanin-enriched microdomains.
source: Furthermore, tetraspanin CD151 regulates integrin activities by influencing their positioning within tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (Berditchevski et al., 2001; Stipp, 2010; Yang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Crowding of CD151 at the sites where virus particles are bound results in co-accumulation of additional virus interacting molecules, laminin and integrin complexes.
source: Crowding of CD151 at the sites where virus particles are bound results in co-accumulation of additional virus interacting molecules, laminin and integrin complexes, which is in line with our previous analysis on CD151 mutants demonstrating the importance of CD151/integrin complex formation in HPV16 infection (Scheffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed CD151 enrichment and cited previous work.

claim: The membrane-associated protein annexin A2 has been identified in virus/GFR complexes and is utilized by many viruses during cell entry, including HPV16.
source: Furthermore, the membrane-associated protein annexin A2 has been identified in virus/GFR complexes and is utilized by many viruses during cell entry, including HPV16 (Mikuličić and Florin, 2019; Dziduszko and Ozbun, 2013; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: ADAM17 acts by the shedding of growth factors that trigger ERK signaling activation and thereby mediate the co-clustering of preformed larger CD151-EGFR microdomains and HPV16 in the plasma membrane.
source: We propose a model in which ADAM17 acts by the shedding of growth factors. These molecules trigger ERK signaling activation and thereby mediate the co-clustering of preformed larger CD151-EGFR microdomains and HPV16 in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a proposed model summarizing the main findings of the study.

claim: ADAM17-mediated events lead to the assembly of a functional virus entry platform, priming of the HPV capsid proteins, endocytosis into the infectious pathway and eventually infection.
source: These events lead to the assembly of a functional virus entry platform, priming of the HPV capsid proteins, endocytosis into the infectious pathway and eventually infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion summarizing the cascade of events identified in the study.
